chapter_summary:
The Raspberry Pi has a dedicated camera connector that supports the official Raspberry Pi Camera Module. Camera modules are available in standard and wide-angle versions, with and without infrared support. The Camera Module 3 adds autofocus. The High Quality Camera supports interchangeable lenses.

Before using the camera, enable the camera interface in `raspi-config` under Interface Options. On Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm and later, the recommended Python library is `picamera2`. On older systems, the legacy `picamera` library was used.

Capture a still image:

```python
from picamera2 import Picamera2
from time import sleep

camera = Picamera2()
camera.start()
sleep(2)  # allow time for auto exposure
camera.capture_file("image.jpg")
camera.stop()
print("Image saved")
```

Capture video:

```python
from picamera2 import Picamera2

camera = Picamera2()
camera.start_and_record_video("video.mp4", duration=10)
```

For basic computer vision, you can combine the camera with OpenCV. OpenCV can detect faces, track colors, and perform many other vision tasks. It can be installed with:

```bash
sudo apt install python3-opencv
```

A simple motion detection project compares frames and detects changes:

```python
import cv2
from picamera2 import Picamera2
from gpiozero import MotionSensor

pir = MotionSensor(18)
camera = Picamera2()
camera.start()

while True:
    pir.wait_for_motion()
    frame = camera.capture_array()
    cv2.imwrite("motion.jpg", frame)
    print("Motion captured")
    pir.wait_for_no_motion()
```

Computer vision projects can be computationally intensive. The Raspberry Pi 4 and Pi 5 handle basic OpenCV tasks well, but complex deep-learning models may require optimization or an accelerator such as the Coral USB Accelerator.

screens.title: Raspberry Pi Camera Module
screens.subtitle: Install, enable, capture, and add simple computer vision

narration.text: This chapter introduces the Raspberry Pi Camera Module and the practical steps you need to install and use it for photos, video, and basic computer vision. You will learn which camera variants exist, how to enable the interface on Raspberry Pi OS, and the recommended Python library for modern systems. Then we’ll show code patterns for taking still images and recording video using picamera2, explain how to hand frames to OpenCV for tasks like face detection or color tracking, and walk through a simple motion-triggered camera example using a PIR sensor. I’ll also point out a few common pitfalls: connector orientation and forgetting to enable the camera in raspi-config, the short initial exposure delay before capturing, and the performance limits when you try to run heavy neural models on a small board. By the end you should be able to connect a camera, run a short capture script, add a basic OpenCV overlay, and plan when an accelerator is needed. Think about one project you might build: a door camera, a wildlife monitor, or an experiment in color tracking. What will your first capture look like?

screens.title: Camera Module Variants
screens.subtitle: Standard, wide-angle, infrared, autofocus, and High Quality models

narration.text: The Raspberry Pi Camera Module family includes several variants, each designed for different use cases. Standard and wide-angle modules provide compact, board-mounted cameras for general photography and video. Infrared-capable modules allow low-light or night use when paired with IR illumination. The Camera Module 3 adds autofocus so it can handle variable subject distance better. The High Quality Camera is a larger module with an interchangeable lens mount for projects that require optical zoom, manual focus, or high-clarity optics. When choosing a module, match the physical constraints and your imaging needs: compact modules are ideal for tight enclosures and simple monitoring, while the High Quality Camera fits experiments requiring different lenses. A common misconception is that all modules behave the same; in practice the optical characteristics and lens options affect exposure, field of view, and focus behavior. For example, infrared modules may need color correction in daytime color images. Consider power, space, and whether you need autofocus before you pick a model. What imaging trade-off matters most for your project — size, field of view, or lens flexibility? Camera Module Variants means select a camera variant that fits the project's space and optical needs: small modules for compact projects, hq for lens flexibility, and camera module 3 for autofocus.. In practical terms, standard, wide-angle, infrared, autofocus, and high quality models. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Connector Orientation and Physical Installation
screens.subtitle: How to seat the flex cable and secure the module safely

narration.text: Correct physical installation is the first thing to verify before debugging software. The camera uses a dedicated CSI camera connector: a small, flat flex cable that plugs into the board. The orientation matters — the cable's exposed conductors must face the board contacts when inserted in the connector clamp. Gently lift the connector latch, insert the flex cable fully, and then close the latch to secure it. If the connector is not fully seated or the latch is not shut, the camera will not be detected. Secure the camera module to your case or header with the provided hardware so the cable does not strain the connector. A frequent mistake is forcing the cable in rotated 180 degrees or leaving the latch half-closed. Another problem is reversing power while connecting add-on hardware; always attach and orient components with power removed when possible. After installation, boot the Pi and enable the camera in raspi-config under Interface Options. If the OS still does not see the camera, re-check seating and try another cable if available. Proper installation reduces a majority of physical connectivity issues and saves debugging time.

keyIdea.title: Orientation matters
keyIdea.text: Insert the flex cable with conductors facing the board contacts and lock the clamp. Secure the module to avoid cable strain.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Connector Orientation
Procedure

Seat the CSI flex cable correctly

  1. Power down the Raspberry Pi before connecting hardware when possible.
  2. Lift the small connector latch on the CSI socket gently.
  3. Insert the camera flex cable fully, with the exposed conductor side facing the board contacts.
  4. Close the latch to clamp the cable and secure the module in place.
  5. Fasten the module so the cable is not strained during use.
Common mistakes
  • Rotating the cable 180 degrees so conductors face away from the contacts.
  • Leaving the latch open or only partially closed.
  • Allowing cable strain that loosens the connector over time.
Pro tip
If the camera isn’t detected after boot, power down, reseat the cable, and try again before changing software settings.

narration.text: A simple, reliable pattern for taking a photo uses picamera2 to start the camera, wait a short period for auto exposure to settle, then write the frame to a file. screens.subtitle: Use a PIR sensor and gpiozero to capture on motion

narration.text: A simple motion-triggered camera connects a PIR motion sensor to a GPIO pin and uses gpiozero to wait for motion. The pattern in the chapter shows creating a MotionSensor on pin 18, starting the Picamera2 camera, then entering a loop where the code waits for motion, captures an array, writes it to disk with OpenCV, and waits for motion to end before looping again. This approach records snapshots only when movement occurs, saving storage and focusing captures on events of interest. The example demonstrates the essential control flow and uses cv2. imwrite to save motion. jpg. Be aware that PIR sensors have a sensitivity and cooldown behavior; you may need to tune placement and angle for reliable triggers. A common mistake is writing very large images on each trigger without rotation or compression, which can fill an SD card quickly. Add naming conventions or timestamps to saved files and consider a rolling archive to manage storage. This project is an excellent first automation using both sensors and camera capture. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.6 › Motion-triggered Camera
Example code
import cv2
from picamera2 import Picamera2
from gpiozero import MotionSensor

pir = MotionSensor(18)
camera = Picamera2()
camera.start()

while True:
    pir.wait_for_motion()
    frame = camera.capture_array()
    cv2.imwrite("motion.jpg", frame)
    print("Motion captured")
    pir.wait_for_no_motion()
This loop waits for motion, saves a snapshot, and waits for motion to stop before continuing. Add timestamps to filenames in a real project.
Setup tips
  • Place the PIR sensor with a clear view of the monitored area.
  • Test sensitivity and cooldown to avoid rapid false triggers.
  • Use timestamped filenames and file rotation to manage storage.
Common mistake

Saving large uncompressed images on every trigger can quickly exhaust storage; plan filenames and rotation.

screens.title: Performance Considerations and Accelerators
screens.subtitle: What the Pi can do and when to add an accelerator

narration.text: Raspberry Pi models like the Pi 4 and Pi 5 handle basic OpenCV tasks well — face detection, color tracking, and simple frame processing are within their capabilities. However, complex deep-learning models, high-resolution realtime inference, or sustained heavy workloads can overwhelm the Pi's C P U and memory. The chapter cautions that for such demanding tasks you should consider optimization strategies or external accelerators such as the Coral USB Accelerator. Optimizations can include reducing frame size, lowering processing frequency, or using more efficient models. An accelerator offloads neural inference to a device designed for that purpose, improving throughput and freeing the Pi for other tasks. A common misunderstanding is that the Pi can scale linearly by just increasing resolution; instead, C P U and input and output limits often create bottlenecks. Start by profiling your workload: test frame rate and C P U usage with your target resolution and model. If C P U usage is consistently high and latency matters, plan for an accelerator or server-based inference. This trade-off will guide whether to keep processing locally or move heavier workloads off the Pi.

keyIdea.title: Match workload to hardware
keyIdea.text: Pi 4 and Pi 5 are fine for basic vision tasks; add optimization or a USB accelerator like Coral for heavier deep-learning inference.
